entries.content_plain: 3-11. Illustration more at large of Ec 2:1 , 2 . I sought-- I resolved, after search into many plans. give myself unto wine-- literally, "to draw my flesh," or "body to wine" (including all banquetings). Image from a captive drawn after a chariot in triumph ( Ro 6:16 , 19 ; 1Co 12:2 ); or, one "allured" ( 2Pe 2:18 , 19). yet acquainting ... wisdom-- literally, "and my heart (still) was behaving, or guiding itself," with wisdom [Gesenius]. Maurer translates: "was weary of (worldly) wisdom." But the end of Ec 2:9 confirms English Version. folly-- namely, pleasures of the flesh, termed "mad," Ec 2:2 . all the days, &c.-- (See Margin and Ec 6:12 ; Job 15:20 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8007"/><div sID="gen12415" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8007"/>12. He had tried (worldly) wisdom (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.12-Eccl.1.18">Ec 1:12-18</reference>) and folly (foolish pleasure) (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.1-Eccl.2.11">Ec 2:1-11</reference>); he now compares them (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.12">Ec 2:12</reference>) and finds that while (worldly)<div eID="gen12415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12416" type="x-p"/> wisdom excelleth folly (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.13">Ec 2:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.14">14</reference>), yet the one event, death, befalls both (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.14-Eccl.2.16">Ec 2:14-16</reference>), and that thus the wealth acquired by the wise man's "labor" may descend to a "fool" that hath not labored (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.18">Ec 2:18</reference>, 19, 21); therefore all his labor is vanity (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.22">Ec 2:22</reference>, 23).<div eID="gen12416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12417" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">what can the man do ... already done--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.9">Ec 1:9</reference>). Parenthetical. A future investigator can strike nothing out "new," so as to draw a different conclusion from what I draw by comparing "wisdom and madness." Holden, with less ellipsis, translates, "What, O man, shall come after the king?" &c. Better, Grotius, "What man can come after (compete with) the king in the things which are done?" None ever can have the same means of testing what all earthly things can do towards satisfying the soul; namely, worldly wisdom, science, riches, power, longevity, all combined. <div eID="gen12417" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8008"/><div sID="gen12418" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8008"/>13-14. (<reference osisRef="Prov.17.24">Pr 17:24</reference>). The worldly "wise" man has good sense in managing his affairs, skill and taste in building and planting, and keeps within safe and respectable bounds in pleasure, while the "fool" is wanting in these respects ("darkness," equivalent to fatal error, blind infatuation), yet one event, death, happens to both (<reference osisRef="Job.21.26">Job 21:26</reference>). <div eID="gen12418" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8012"/><div sID="gen12427" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8012"/>18-19. One hope alone was left to the disappointed worldling, the perpetuation of his name and riches, laboriously gathered, through his successor. For selfishness is mostly at the root of worldly parents' alleged providence for their children. But now the remembrance of how he himself, the piously reared child of David, had disregarded his father's dying charge (<reference osisRef="1Chr.28.9">1Ch 28:9</reference>), suggested the sad misgivings as to what Rehoboam, his son by an idolatrous Ammonitess, Naamah, should prove to be; a foreboding too fully realized (1Ki 12:1-18; 14:21-31). <div eID="gen12427" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8017"/><div sID="gen12434" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8017"/>24. English Version gives a seemingly Epicurean sense, contrary to the general scope. The Hebrew, literally is, "It is not good for man that he should eat," &c., "and should make his soul see good" (or "show his soul, that is, himself, happy"), &c. [Weiss]. According to Holden and Weiss, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.12">Ec 3:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.22">22</reference> differ from this verse in the text and meaning; here he means, "It is not good that a man should feast himself, and falsely make as though his soul were happy"; he thus refers to a false pretending of happiness acquired by and for one's self; in <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.12">Ec 3:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.22">22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.18">5:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.19">19</reference>, to real seeing, or finding pleasure when God gives it. There it is said to be good for a man to enjoy with satisfaction and thankfulness the blessings which God gives; here it is said not to be good to take an unreal pleasure to one's self by feasting, &c.<div eID="gen12434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12435" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">This also I saw--</hi>I perceived by experience that good (real pleasure) is not to be taken at will, but comes only from the hand of God [Weiss] (<reference osisRef="Ps.4.6">Psa 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.57.19-Isa.57.21">Is 57:19-21</reference>). Or as Holden, "It is the appointment from the hand of God, that the sensualist has no solid satisfaction" (good). <div eID="gen12435" type="x-p"/>

According to Holden and Weiss, Ec 3:12 , 22 differ from this verse in the text and meaning; here he means, "It is not good that a man should feast himself, and falsely make as though his soul were happy"; he thus refers to a false pretending of happiness acquired by and for one's self; in Ec 3:12 , 22 ; 5:18 , 19 , to real seeing, or finding pleasure when God gives it. There it is said to be good for a man to enjoy with satisfaction and thankfulness the blessings which God gives; here it is said not to be good to take an unreal pleasure to one's self by feasting, &c. Or as Holden, "It is the appointment from the hand of God, that the sensualist has no solid satisfaction" (good).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8018"/><div sID="gen12436" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8018"/><hi type="bold">25. hasten--</hi>after indulgences (<reference osisRef="Prov.7.23">Pr 7:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.19.2">19:2</reference>), eagerly pursue such enjoyments. None can compete with me in this. If I, then, with all my opportunities of enjoyment, failed utterly to obtain solid pleasure of my own making, apart from God, who else can? God mercifully spares His children the sad experiment which Solomon made, by denying them the goods which they often desire. He gives them the fruits of Solomon's experience, without their paying the dear price at which Solomon bought it. <div eID="gen12436" type="x-p"/>
